summary: Introduces Dual-Stack Lite, which helps broadband providers share IPv4 addresses among customers while rolling out IPv6. It combines two familiar techniques, tunneling IPv4 inside IPv6 and network address translation, to better balance the costs and benefits of IPv6 deployment.

eli5.summary: Your home network sends old-style internet traffic through a pipe of the newer kind to the provider, where many homes share a few old addresses. This lets providers go IPv6 without running out of IPv4.

subtitle: How a broadband provider can run an IPv6-only access network and still share scarce IPv4 addresses among customers.

tldr.problem: The IANA free pool of IPv4 addresses ran out before IPv6 was widely deployed, yet providers still have to keep IPv4 services working with very little address space.
tldr.mechanism: Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) carries customers' IPv4 packets inside IPv6 tunnels from a B4 element in the home to an AFTR in the provider network, where a carrier-grade IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT shares public addresses.
tldr.outcome: The provider can run IPv6 only up to the customer premises while customers keep IPv4. The cost is NAT in the core, with its limits on logging, ALGs and port usage. RFC 7335 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 6333 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7335. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Dual-Stack Lite Exists
sections.content:
For more than ten years the common plan was that the move to IPv6 would happen purely through the dual-stack model, with most things converted before IPv4 ran out. The RFC notes that this did not happen: the IANA free pool of IPv4 addresses has been depleted well before enough IPv6 deployment took place.

Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) is the answer. It combines two well-known technologies, IPv4-in-IPv6 tunneling and Network Address Translation (NAT), so that a broadband service provider can share IPv4 addresses among customers. It also decouples IPv6 deployment in the provider network from the rest of the Internet, which makes incremental deployment easier.

The RFC makes a distinction between a dual-stack-capable device (it has code for both IPv4 and IPv6) and a dual-stack-provisioned device (it has been given both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address). Pure IPv6-only devices, with no IPv4 stack, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: The world ran out of the old kind of addresses before everyone had switched to the new kind. DS-Lite is a way to keep old-style traffic working while providers move to the new kind.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Instead of stacking one NAT behind another, DS-Lite builds IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels that cross the provider network to a carrier-grade IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT, called the AFTR, where customers share IPv4 addresses. The RFC lists several benefits: IPv6 in the provider network is decoupled from IPv6 in the global Internet; access networks are simpler because overlapping private IPv4 spaces are not needed for very large customer bases; tunnels can end anywhere, which allows horizontal scaling; and the direct tunnel lets customers influence how the AFTR performs its NAT.

Communication stays within one address family. IPv6 sources only talk to IPv6 destinations and IPv4 sources only to IPv4 destinations, with no protocol family translation. That keeps life simple for applications that carry literal IP addresses in their payloads.

Two scenarios are described. In the first, a home gateway (the CPE) is provisioned only with IPv6 by the provider and has a B4 interface on its WAN side. It SHOULD NOT run a NAT between the home network and the B4 interface, to avoid double NAT. It SHOULD run a DHCP(v4) server handing out RFC 1918 addresses, advertise itself as default IPv4 router and DNS server, and run a DNS proxy. In the second, a device is connected straight to the modem, is provisioned with IPv6 only, and acts as the B4 element itself. In both cases IPv6 traffic simply follows normal IPv6 routing and does not use the tunnel.
sections.eli5: Instead of every house having its own small gate onto the street, all the houses send their old-style mail through one covered tunnel to a big post office that shares out a few street addresses.

sections.title: The B4 Element
sections.content:
The B4 (Basic Bridging BroadBand) element is a function on a dual-stack-capable node, either a CPE or a directly connected device, that creates a tunnel to an AFTR. The tunnel is a multipoint-to-point IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel ending on the provider's AFTR. At the time, DS-Lite defined only IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels, though other encapsulations could be defined later.

Fragmentation. Encapsulation shrinks the effective MTU, and path MTU discovery is not a reliable fix. The preferred solution is for the provider to raise the MTU of all links between B4 and AFTR by at least 40 bytes. Where that is impossible, the B4 MUST fragment and reassemble: the inner IPv4 packet MUST NOT be fragmented, fragmentation MUST happen after IPv6 encapsulation, and reassembly MUST happen before decapsulation, following RFC 2473 Section 7.2.

Finding the AFTR. The B4 needs the AFTR's IPv6 address, which can come from out-of-band configuration, manual configuration or DHCPv6 options. For interoperability a B4 SHOULD implement the DHCPv6 option from RFC 6334.

DNS. Because the B4 is configured only with IPv6, it learns DNS recursive servers over IPv6 and performs all DNS resolution over IPv6. It cannot pass that IPv6 address to IPv4 hosts, so it SHOULD implement a DNS proxy following RFC 5625.

Well-known address. IANA defined 192.0.0.0/29 for DS-Lite interfaces. The address 192.0.0.0 is the reserved subnet, 192.0.0.1 is for the AFTR and 192.0.0.2 is for the B4. A B4 MAY use another address in the range if a provider configuration prevents using 192.0.0.2.
sections.eli5: The B4 is the little mail-room in your home that wraps each old-style letter in a new-style envelope and knows the address of the big post office to send it to.

sections.title: The AFTR and Its Binding Table
sections.content:
An AFTR (Address Family Transition Router) is the combination of an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel endpoint and an IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT on the same node. Its tunnel is point-to-multipoint, ending at the B4 elements.

The AFTR must also fragment and reassemble if the link MTU cannot hold the encapsulation. The RFC warns that reassembly at the tunnel exit can be expensive because the AFTR must buffer fragments for many tunnels, but expects it to be only a fraction of the workload, since most clients receive large IPv4 packets rather than send them. When resources run low, the AFTR SHOULD notify the administrator before they are exhausted. DNS traffic is not expected to pass through the AFTR, because B4 elements resolve names over IPv6.

The AFTR SHOULD use 192.0.0.1 to configure its end of the tunnel. That address can report ICMP problems and shows up in traceroute output.

The key trick is the extended binding table. Customers use overlapping private IPv4 addresses, so the AFTR adds the source IPv6 address of incoming packets to each NAT binding to tell them apart. A reverse lookup in that table tells the AFTR how to rebuild the IPv6 encapsulation when packets return from the Internet, so no static per-tunnel configuration is needed.

Tunneling MUST follow RFC 2473 and RFC 4213, and traffic classes from the IPv4 headers MUST be carried over to the IPv6 headers and vice versa. Multicast is out of scope.
sections.eli5: At the big post office, many houses use the same flat numbers. So the clerk writes down which tunnel each letter came from, and that is how replies find the right house.

sections.title: NAT Considerations
sections.content:
The AFTR MAY have several NAT pools, whose address ranges may be disjoint but MUST NOT overlap. Operators can assign different sets of B4s to different pools. The AFTR MUST behave according to the NAT best current practice in RFC 4787, RFC 5508 and RFC 5382.

Because the AFTR does NAT-44, it inherits NAT's limits. Some protocols need application level gateways (ALGs); Active FTP is the RFC's example. ALGs use resources, and a shared device cannot implement every current and future ALG. Sharing one public address among many users also raises issues such as logging and lawful intercept; RFC 6269 covers port sharing in more depth.

For port forwarding and keep-alive traffic, the RFC points to the Port Control Protocol (PCP), then being standardized, which lets applications ask the NAT to open ports and negotiate lifetimes.
sections.eli5: Sharing one address among many houses works, but some old tricks, like a game that needs the post office to deliver straight to your door, can break unless the post office is given extra help.

sections.title: Security and Logging
sections.content:
Moving NAT from the home gateway into the provider core means an IPv4 address and a timestamp no longer identify a customer. The AFTR should therefore be able to log the tunnel identifier, protocol, ports and addresses, and the creation time of each NAT binding. Exactly what is logged is implementation specific.

When decapsulating, the AFTR MUST forward only packets sourced from RFC 1918 addresses, the IANA reserved range, or other out-of-band pre-authorized addresses, and MUST drop everything else. This stops rogue devices from mounting denial-of-service attacks with unauthorized public source addresses; a TCP SYN attack is the RFC's example.

Because ports become a critical shared resource, the AFTR needs a way to limit port usage, either by rate-limiting new connections or by a hard cap on ports per user. The RFC also suggests limiting service to registered customers, for example with an IPv6 ingress filter on the AFTR's tunnel interface. An ISP may also configure the AFTR to bypass translation for specific address, port and protocol combinations.
sections.eli5: When many houses share one address, the post office must keep a careful notebook of who sent what, and must refuse envelopes that claim to come from somewhere they should not.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix B walks through two architectures. In the gateway-based architecture, the home router hands out private addresses and holds the B4. When a host sends an IPv4 datagram, the B4 encapsulates it in an IPv6 datagram to the AFTR instead of doing NAT itself. The AFTR decapsulates it and translates the source address.

In the RFC's example, a host at 10.0.0.1 using TCP source port 10000 talks to 198.51.100.1 on port 80. The home router's WAN address is 2001:db8:0:1::1 and the AFTR's is 2001:db8:0:2::1. The AFTR rewrites the source to 192.0.2.1 and port 5000. Replies go through the reverse translation. The AFTR's table key is the softwire identifier (the CPE's IPv6 address) plus the IPv4 address and port.

In the host-based architecture, a host with only an IPv6 address pre-configures the well-known IPv4 address 192.0.0.2 and sources IPv4 traffic from it. Every such host uses the same IPv4 address, so the AFTR relies entirely on each host's unique IPv6 address to tell them apart.
sections.eli5: The examples follow one letter on its trip: wrapped at home, unwrapped at the post office, restamped with a shared return address, and then the reply makes the same trip backwards.
